or ith princes ho had gold, ho filled their houses ith silver;
or as a hidden untimely birth I had not been, as infants ho never sa light.
There the icked cease from troubling. There the eary are at rest.
There the prisoners are at ease together. They don’t hear the voice of the taskmaster.
The small and the great are there. The servant is free from his master. \b
“ Why is light given to him ho is in misery, life to the bitter in soul,
ho long for death, but it doesn’t come; and dig for it more than for hidden treasures,
ho rejoice exceedingly, and are glad, hen they can find the grave?
Why is light given to a man hose ay is hidden, hom God has hedged in?
For my sighing comes before I eat. My groanings are poured out like ater.
For the thing hich I fear comes on me, that hich I am afraid of comes to me.
I am not at ease, neither am I quiet, neither do I have rest; but trouble comes.”
Then Eliphaz the Temanite ansered,
“If someone ventures to talk ith you, ill you be grieved? But ho can ithhold himself from speaking?
Behold, you have instructed many, you have strengthened the eak hands.
Your ords have supported him ho as falling, you have made the feeble knees firm.
But no it has come to you, and you faint. It touches you, and you are troubled.
Isn’t your piety your confidence? Isn’t the integrity of your ays your hope? \b
“ Remember, no, ho ever perished, being innocent? Or here ere the upright cut off?
According to hat I have seen, those ho plo iniquity and so trouble, reap the same.
By the breath of God they perish. By the blast of his anger are they consumed.
The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions, are broken.
The old lion perishes for lack of prey. The cubs of the lioness are scattered abroad. \b
“ No a thing as secretly brought to me. My ear received a hisper of it.
In thoughts from the visions of the night, hen deep sleep falls on men,
fear came on me, and trembling, hich made all my bones shake.
Then a spirit passed before my face. The hair of my flesh stood up.
It stood still, but I couldn’t discern its appearance. A form as before my eyes. Silence, then I heard a voice, saying,
’ Shall mortal man be more just than God? Shall a man be more pure than his Maker?
Behold, he puts no trust in his servants. He charges his angels ith error.
Ho much more those ho dell in houses of clay, hose foundation is in the dust, ho are crushed before the moth!
Beteen morning and evening they are destroyed. They perish forever ithout any regarding it.
Isn’t their tent cord plucked up ithin them? They die, and that ithout isdom.’
“ Call no; is there any ho ill anser you? To hich of the holy ones ill you turn?
For resentment kills the foolish man, and jealousy kills the simple.
I have seen the foolish taking root, but suddenly I cursed his habitation.
His children are far from safety. They are crushed in the gate. Neither is there any to deliver them,
hose harvest the hungry eat up, and take it even out of the thorns. The snare gapes for their substance.
For affliction doesn’t come out of the dust, neither does trouble spring out of the ground;
but man is born to trouble, as the sparks fly upard. \b
“But as for me, I ould seek God. I ould commit my cause to God,
ho does great things that can’t be fathomed, marvelous things ithout number;
ho gives rain on the earth, and sends aters on the fields;
so that he sets up on high those ho are lo, those ho mourn are exalted to safety.
He frustrates the plans of the crafty, so that their hands can’t perform their enterprise.
He takes the ise in their on craftiness; the counsel of the cunning is carried headlong.
They meet ith darkness in the day time, and grope at noonday as in the night.
But he saves from the sord of their mouth, even the needy from the hand of the mighty.
So the poor has hope, and injustice shuts her mouth. \b
“ Behold, happy is the man hom God corrects. Therefore do not despise the chastening of the Almighty.
For he ounds and binds up. He injures and his hands make hole.
He ill deliver you in six troubles; yes, in seven no evil ill touch you.
In famine he ill redeem you from death; in ar, from the poer of the sord.
You ill be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, neither ill you be afraid of destruction hen it comes.
You ill laugh at destruction and famine, neither ill you be afraid of the animals of the earth.
For you ill be allied ith the stones of the field. The animals of the field ill be at peace ith you.
You ill kno that your tent is in peace. You ill visit your fold, and ill miss nothing.
You ill kno also that your offspring ill be great, your offspring as the grass of the earth.
You ill come to your grave in a full age, like a shock of grain comes in its season.
Behold, e have researched it. It is so. Hear it, and kno it for your good.” \b
Then Job ansered,
“ Oh that my anguish ere eighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances!
For no it ould be heavier than the sand of the seas, therefore my ords have been rash.
For the arros of the Almighty are ithin me. My spirit drinks up their poison. The terrors of God set themselves in array against me.
Does the ild donkey bray hen he has grass? Or does the ox lo over his fodder?
Can that hich has no flavor be eaten ithout salt? Or is there any taste in the hite of an egg?
My soul refuses to touch them. They are as loathsome food to me. \b
“ Oh that I might have my request, that God ould grant the thing that I long for,
even that it ould please God to crush me; that he ould let loose his hand, and cut me off!
Let it still be my consolation, yes, let me exult in pain that doesn’t spare, that I have not denied the ords of the Holy One.
What is my strength, that I should ait? What is my end, that I should be patient?
Is my strength the strength of stones? Or is my flesh of bronze?
Isn’t it that I have no help in me, that isdom is driven aay from me? \b
“ To him ho is ready to faint, kindness should be shon from his friend; even to him ho forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
My brothers have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the channel of brooks that pass aay;
hich are black by reason of the ice, in hich the sno hides itself.
In the dry season, they vanish. When it is hot, they are consumed out of their place.
The caravans that travel beside them turn aay. They go up into the aste, and perish.
The caravans of Tema looked. The companies of Sheba aited for them.
They ere distressed because they ere confident. They came there, and ere confounded.
For no you are nothing. You see a terror, and are afraid.
Did I ever say, ’ Give to me’? or, ’ Offer a present for me from your substance’?
or, ’ Deliver me from the adversary’s hand’? or, ’ Redeem me from the hand of the oppressors’? \b
“ Teach me, and I ill hold my peace. Cause me to understand my error.
Ho forcible are ords of uprightness! But your reproof, hat does it reprove?
Do you intend to reprove ords, since the speeches of one ho is desperate are as ind?
Yes, you ould even cast lots for the fatherless, and make merchandise of your friend.
No therefore be pleased to look at me, for surely I ill not lie to your face.
Please return. Let there be no injustice. Yes, return again. My cause is righteous.
Is there injustice on my tongue? Can’t my taste discern mischievous things?
“Isn’t a man forced to labor on earth? Aren’t his days like the days of a hired hand?
As a servant ho earnestly desires the shado, as a hireling ho looks for his ages,
so I am made to possess months of misery, earisome nights are appointed to me.
When I lie don, I say, ’ When ill I arise, and the night be gone?’ I toss and turn until the daning of the day.
My flesh is clothed ith orms and clods of dust. My skin closes up, and breaks out afresh.
My days are sifter than a eaver’s shuttle, and are spent ithout hope.
Oh remember that my life is a breath. My eye ill no more see good.
The eye of him ho sees me ill see me no more. Your eyes ill be on me, but I ill not be.
As the cloud is consumed and vanishes aay, so he ho goes don to Sheol ill come up no more.
He ill return no more to his house, neither ill his place kno him any more. \b
“ Therefore I ill not keep silent. I ill speak in the anguish of my spirit. I ill complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Am I a sea, or a sea monster, that you put a guard over me?
When I say, ’ My bed ill comfort me. My couch ill ease my complaint,’
then you scare me ith dreams and terrify me through visions,
so that my soul chooses strangling, death rather than my bones.
I loathe my life. I don’t ant to live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath.
What is man, that you should magnify him, that you should set your mind on him,
that you should visit him every morning, and test him every moment?
Ho long ill you not look aay from me, nor leave me alone until I sallo don my spittle?
If I have sinned, hat do I do to you, you atcher of men? Why have you set me as a mark for you, so that I am a burden to myself?
Why do you not pardon my disobedience, and take aay my iniquity? For no ill I lie don in the dust. You ill seek me diligently, but I ill not be.”
Then Bildad the Shuhite ansered,
“ Ho long ill you speak these things? Shall the ords of your mouth be a mighty ind?
Does God pervert justice? Or does the Almighty pervert righteousness?
If your children have sinned against him, he has delivered them into the hand of their disobedience.
If you ant to seek God diligently, make your supplication to the Almighty.
If you ere pure and upright, surely no he ould aaken for you, and make the habitation of your righteousness prosperous.
Though your beginning as small, yet your latter end ould greatly increase. \b
“ Please inquire of past generations. Find out about the learning of their fathers.
( For e are but of yesterday, and kno nothing, because our days on earth are a shado.)
Shall they not teach you, tell you, and utter ords out of their heart? \b
“ Can the papyrus gro up ithout mire? Can the rushes gro ithout ater?
While it is yet in its greenness, not cut don, it ithers before any other reed.
So are the paths of all ho forget God. The hope of the godless man ill perish,
hose confidence ill break apart, hose trust is a spider’s eb.
He ill lean on his house, but it ill not stand. He ill cling to it, but it ill not endure.
He is green before the sun. His shoots go out along his garden.
His roots are rapped around the rock pile. He sees the place of stones.
If he is destroyed from his place, then it ill deny him, saying, ’ I have not seen you.’
Behold, this is the joy of his ay. Out of the earth, others ill spring. \b
“ Behold, God ill not cast aay a blameless man, neither ill he uphold the evildoers.
He ill still fill your mouth ith laughter, your lips ith shouting.
Those ho hate you ill be clothed ith shame. The tent of the icked ill be no more.”
Then Job ansered,
“ Truly I kno that it is so, but ho can man be just ith God?
If he is pleased to contend ith him, he can’t anser him one time in a thousand.
God is ise in heart, and mighty in strength. Who has hardened himself against him and prospered?
He removes the mountains, and they don’t kno it, hen he overturns them in his anger.
He shakes the earth out of its place. Its pillars tremble.
He commands the sun and it doesn’t rise, and seals up the stars.
He alone stretches out the heavens, and treads on the aves of the sea.
He makes the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades, and the rooms of the south.
He does great things past finding out; yes, marvelous things ithout number.
Behold, he goes by me, and I don’t see him. He passes on also, but I don’t perceive him.
Behold, he snatches aay. Who can hinder him? Who ill ask him, ’ What are you doing?’ \b
“ God ill not ithdra his anger. The helpers of Rahab stoop under him.
Ho much less ill I anser him, and choose my ords to argue ith him?
Though I ere righteous, yet I ouldn’t anser him. I ould make supplication to my judge.
If I had called, and he had ansered me, yet I ouldn’t believe that he listened to my voice.
For he breaks me ith a storm, and multiplies my ounds ithout cause.
He ill not allo me to catch my breath, but fills me ith bitterness.
If it is a matter of strength, behold, he is mighty! If of justice, ’ Who,’ says he, ’ ill summon me?’
Though I am righteous, my on mouth ill condemn me. Though I am blameless, it ill prove me perverse.
I am blameless. I don’t respect myself. I despise my life. \b
“ It is all the same. Therefore I say he destroys the blameless and the icked.
If the scourge kills suddenly, he ill mock at the trial of the innocent.
The earth is given into the hand of the icked. He covers the faces of its judges. If not he, then ho is it? \b
“ No my days are sifter than a runner. They flee aay. They see no good.
They have passed aay as the sift ships, as the eagle that soops on the prey.
If I say, ’ I ill forget my complaint, I ill put off my sad face, and cheer up,’
I am afraid of all my sorros. I kno that you ill not hold me innocent.
I ill be condemned. Why then do I labor in vain?
If I ash myself ith sno, and cleanse my hands ith lye,
yet you ill plunge me in the ditch. My on clothes ill abhor me.
For he is not a man, as I am, that I should anser him, that e should come together in judgment.
There is no umpire beteen us, that might lay his hand on us both.
Let him take his rod aay from me. Let his terror not make me afraid;
then I ould speak, and not fear him, for I am not so in myself. \b
“ My soul is eary of my life. I ill give free course to my complaint. I ill speak in the bitterness of my soul.
I ill tell God, ’ Do not condemn me. Sho me hy you contend ith me.
Is it good to you that you should oppress, that you should despise the ork of your hands, and smile on the counsel of the icked?
Do you have eyes of flesh? Or do you see as man sees?
Are your days as the days of mortals, or your years as man’s years,
that you inquire after my iniquity, and search after my sin?
Although you kno that I am not icked, there is no one ho can deliver out of your hand. \b
“’ Your hands have framed me and fashioned me altogether, yet you destroy me.
Remember, I beg you, that you have fashioned me as clay. Will you bring me into dust again?
Haven’t you poured me out like milk, and curdled me like cheese?
You have clothed me ith skin and flesh, and knit me together ith bones and sines.
You have granted me life and loving kindness. Your visitation has preserved my spirit.
Yet you hid these things in your heart. I kno that this is ith you:
if I sin, then you mark me. You ill not acquit me from my iniquity.
If I am icked, oe to me. If I am righteous, I still ill not lift up my head, being filled ith disgrace, and conscious of my affliction.
If my head is held high, you hunt me like a lion. Again you sho yourself poerful to me.
You rene your itnesses against me, and increase your indignation on me. Changes and arfare are ith me. \b
“’ Why, then, have you brought me out of the omb? I ish I had given up the spirit, and no eye had seen me.
I should have been as though I had not been. I should have been carried from the omb to the grave.
Aren’t my days fe? Stop! Leave me alone, that I may find a little comfort,
before I go here I ill not return from, to the land of darkness and of the shado of death;
the land dark as midnight, of the shado of death, ithout any order, here the light is as midnight.’”
Then Zophar, the Naamathite, ansered,
“Shouldn’t the multitude of ords be ansered? Should a man full of talk be justified?
Should your boastings make men hold their peace? When you mock, ill no man make you ashamed?
For you say, ’ My doctrine is pure. I am clean in your eyes.’
But oh that God ould speak, and open his lips against you,
that he ould sho you the secrets of isdom! For true isdom has to sides. Kno therefore that God exacts of you less than your iniquity deserves. \b
“Can you fathom the mystery of God? Or can you probe the limits of the Almighty?
They are high as heaven. What can you do? They are deeper than Sheol. What can you kno?
Its measure is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.
If he passes by, or confines, or convenes a court, then ho can oppose him?
For he knos false men. He sees iniquity also, even though he doesn’t consider it.
An empty-headed man becomes ise hen a man is born as a ild donkey’s colt. \b
“If you set your heart aright, stretch out your hands toard him.
If iniquity is in your hand, put it far aay. Don’t let unrighteousness dell in your tents.
Surely then you ill lift up your face ithout spot. Yes, you ill be steadfast, and ill not fear,
for you ill forget your misery. You ill remember it like aters that have passed aay.
Life ill be clearer than the noonday. Though there is darkness, it ill be as the morning.
You ill be secure, because there is hope. Yes, you ill search, and ill take your rest in safety.
Also you ill lie don, and no one ill make you afraid. Yes, many ill court your favor.
But the eyes of the icked ill fail. They ill have no ay to flee. Their hope ill be the giving up of the spirit.”
Then Job ansered,
“No doubt, but you are the people, and isdom ill die ith you.
But I have understanding as ell as you; I am not inferior to you. Yes, ho doesn’t kno such things as these?
I am like one ho is a joke to his neighbor, I, ho called on God, and he ansered. The just, the blameless man is a joke.
In the thought of him ho is at ease there is contempt for misfortune. It is ready for them hose foot slips.
The tents of robbers prosper. Those ho provoke God are secure, ho carry their god in their hands. \b
“But ask the animals no, and they ill teach you; the birds of the sky, and they ill tell you.
Or speak to the earth, and it ill teach you. The fish of the sea ill declare to you.
Who doesn’t kno that in all these, the LORD’s hand has done this,
in hose hand is the life of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind?
Doesn’t the ear try ords, even as the palate tastes its food?
With aged men is isdom, in length of days understanding. \b
“ With God is isdom and might. He has counsel and understanding.
Behold, he breaks don, and it can’t be built again. He imprisons a man, and there can be no release.
Behold, he ithholds the aters, and they dry up. Again, he sends them out, and they overturn the earth.
With him is strength and isdom. The deceived and the deceiver are his.
He leads counselors aay stripped. He makes judges fools.
He loosens the bond of kings. He binds their aist ith a belt.
He leads priests aay stripped, and overthros the mighty.
He removes the speech of those ho are trusted, and takes aay the understanding of the elders.
He pours contempt on princes, and loosens the belt of the strong.
He uncovers deep things out of darkness, and brings out to light the shado of death.
He increases the nations, and he destroys them. He enlarges the nations, and he leads them captive.
He takes aay understanding from the chiefs of the people of the earth, and causes them to ander in a ilderness here there is no ay.
They grope in the dark ithout light. He makes them stagger like a drunken man. \b
“ Behold, my eye has seen all this. My ear has heard and understood it.
What you kno, I kno also. I am not inferior to you. \b
“ Surely I ould speak to the Almighty. I desire to reason ith God.
But you are forgers of lies. You are all physicians of no value.
Oh that you ould be completely silent! Then you ould be ise.
Hear no my reasoning. Listen to the pleadings of my lips.
Will you speak unrighteously for God, and talk deceitfully for him?
Will you sho partiality to him? Will you contend for God?
Is it good that he should search you out? Or as one deceives a man, ill you deceive him?
He ill surely reprove you if you secretly sho partiality.
Won’t his majesty make you afraid and his dread fall on you?
Your memorable sayings are proverbs of ashes. Your defenses are defenses of clay. \b
“ Be silent! Leave me alone, that I may speak. Let come on me hat ill.
Why should I take my flesh in my teeth, and put my life in my hand?
Behold, he ill kill me. I have no hope. Nevertheless, I ill maintain my ays before him.
This also ill be my salvation, that a godless man ill not come before him.
Listen carefully to my speech. Let my declaration be in your ears.
See no, I have set my cause in order. I kno that I am righteous.
Who is he ho ill contend ith me? For then I ould hold my peace and give up the spirit. \b
“Only don’t do to things to me, then I ill not hide myself from your face:
ithdra your hand far from me, and don’t let your terror make me afraid.
Then call, and I ill anser, or let me speak, and you anser me.
Ho many are my iniquities and sins? Make me kno my disobedience and my sin.
Why do you hide your face, and consider me your enemy?
Will you harass a driven leaf? Will you pursue the dry stubble?
For you rite bitter things against me, and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.
You also put my feet in the stocks, and mark all my paths. You set a bound to the soles of my feet,
though I am decaying like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten. \b
“ Man, ho is born of a oman, is of fe days, and full of trouble.
He gros up like a floer, and is cut don. He also flees like a shado, and doesn’t continue.
Do you open your eyes on such a one, and bring me into judgment ith you?
Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? Not one.
Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months is ith you, and you have appointed his bounds that he can’t pass.
Look aay from him, that he may rest, until he accomplishes, as a hireling, his day. \b
“ For there is hope for a tree if it is cut don, that it ill sprout again, that the tender branch of it ill not cease.
Though its root gros old in the earth, and its stock dies in the ground,
yet through the scent of ater it ill bud, and sprout boughs like a plant.
But man dies, and is laid lo. Yes, man gives up the spirit, and here is he?
As the aters fail from the sea, and the river astes and dries up,
so man lies don and doesn’t rise. Until the heavens are no more, they ill not aake, nor be roused out of their sleep. \b
“ Oh that you ould hide me in Sheol, that you ould keep me secret until your rath is past, that you ould appoint me a set time and remember me!
If a man dies, ill he live again? I ould ait all the days of my arfare, until my release should come.
You ould call, and I ould anser you. You ould have a desire for the ork of your hands.
But no you count my steps. Don’t you atch over my sin?
My disobedience is sealed up in a bag. You fasten up my iniquity. \b
“But the mountain falling comes to nothing. The rock is removed out of its place.
The aters ear the stones. The torrents of it ash aay the dust of the earth. So you destroy the hope of man.
You forever prevail against him, and he departs. You change his face, and send him aay.
His sons come to honor, and he doesn’t kno it. They are brought lo, but he doesn’t perceive it of them.
But his flesh on him has pain, and his soul ithin him mourns.” \b
Then Eliphaz the Temanite ansered,
“ Should a ise man anser ith vain knoledge, and fill himself ith the east ind?
Should he reason ith unprofitable talk, or ith speeches ith hich he can do no good?
Yes, you do aay ith fear, and hinder devotion before God.
For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the language of the crafty.
Your on mouth condemns you, and not I. Yes, your on lips testify against you. \b
“ Are you the first man ho as born? Or ere you brought out before the hills?
Have you heard the secret counsel of God? Do you limit isdom to yourself?
What do you kno that e don’t kno? What do you understand hich is not in us?
With us are both the gray-headed and the very aged men, much older than your father.
Are the consolations of God too small for you, even the ord that is gentle toard you?
Why does your heart carry you aay? Why do your eyes flash,
that you turn your spirit against God, and let such ords go out of your mouth?
What is man, that he should be clean? What is he ho is born of a oman, that he should be righteous?
Behold, he puts no trust in his holy ones. Yes, the heavens are not clean in his sight;
ho much less one ho is abominable and corrupt, a man ho drinks iniquity like ater! \b
“ I ill sho you, listen to me; that hich I have seen I ill declare
(hich ise men have told by their fathers, and have not hidden it;
to hom alone the land as given, and no stranger passed among them):
the icked man rithes in pain all his days, even the number of years that are laid up for the oppressor.
A sound of terrors is in his ears. In prosperity the destroyer ill come on him.
He doesn’t believe that he ill return out of darkness. He is aited for by the sord.
He anders abroad for bread, saying, ’ Where is it?’ He knos that the day of darkness is ready at his hand.
Distress and anguish make him afraid. They prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle.
Because he has stretched out his hand against God, and behaves himself proudly against the Almighty,
he runs at him ith a stiff neck, ith the thick shields of his bucklers,
because he has covered his face ith his fatness, and gathered fat on his thighs.
He has lived in desolate cities, in houses hich no one inhabited, hich ere ready to become heaps.
He ill not be rich, neither ill his substance continue, neither ill their possessions be extended on the earth.
He ill not depart out of darkness. The flame ill dry up his branches. He ill go aay by the breath of God’s mouth.
Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, for emptiness ill be his reard.
It ill be accomplished before his time. His branch ill not be green.
He ill shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and ill cast off his floer as the olive tree.
For the company of the godless ill be barren, and fire ill consume the tents of bribery.
They conceive mischief and produce iniquity. Their heart prepares deceit.” \b
Then Job ansered,
“ I have heard many such things. You are all miserable comforters!
Shall vain ords have an end? Or hat provokes you that you anser?
I also could speak as you do. If your soul ere in my soul’s place, I could join ords together against you, and shake my head at you,
but I ould strengthen you ith my mouth. The solace of my lips ould relieve you. \b
“Though I speak, my grief is not subsided. Though I forbear, hat am I eased?
But no, God, you have surely orn me out. You have made all my company desolate.
You have shriveled me up. This is a itness against me. My leanness rises up against me. It testifies to my face.
He has torn me in his rath and persecuted me. He has gnashed on me ith his teeth. My adversary sharpens his eyes on me.
They have gaped on me ith their mouth. They have struck me on the cheek reproachfully. They gather themselves together against me.
God delivers me to the ungodly, and casts me into the hands of the icked.
I as at ease, and he broke me apart. Yes, he has taken me by the neck, and dashed me to pieces. He has also set me up for his target.
His archers surround me. He splits my kidneys apart, and does not spare. He pours out my bile on the ground.
He breaks me ith breach on breach. He runs at me like a giant.
I have seed sackcloth on my skin, and have thrust my horn in the dust.
My face is red ith eeping. Deep darkness is on my eyelids,
although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure. \b
“Earth, don’t cover my blood. Let my cry have no place to rest.
Even no, behold, my itness is in heaven. He ho vouches for me is on high.
My friends scoff at me. My eyes pour out tears to God,
that he ould maintain the right of a man ith God, of a son of man ith his neighbor!
For hen a fe years have come, I ill go the ay of no return. \b
“ My spirit is consumed. My days are extinct and the grave is ready for me.
Surely there are mockers ith me. My eye dells on their provocation. \b
“ No give a pledge. Be collateral for me ith yourself. Who is there ho ill strike hands ith me?
For you have hidden their heart from understanding, therefore you ill not exalt them.
He ho denounces his friends for plunder, even the eyes of his children ill fail. \b
“ But he has made me a byord of the people. They spit in my face.
My eye also is dim by reason of sorro. All my members are as a shado.
Upright men ill be astonished at this. The innocent ill stir himself up against the godless.
Yet the righteous ill hold to his ay. He ho has clean hands ill gro stronger and stronger.
But as for you all, come back. I ill not find a ise man among you.
My days are past. My plans are broken off, as are the thoughts of my heart.
They change the night into day, saying ’ The light is near’ in the presence of darkness.
If I look for Sheol as my house, if I have spread my couch in the darkness,
if I have said to corruption, ’ You are my father,’ and to the orm, ’ My mother,’ and ’ My sister,’
here then is my hope? As for my hope, ho ill see it?
Shall it go don ith me to the gates of Sheol, or descend together into the dust?” \b
Then Bildad the Shuhite ansered,
“ Ho long ill you hunt for ords? Consider, and afterards e ill speak.
Why are e counted as animals, hich have become unclean in your sight?
You ho tear yourself in your anger, ill the earth be forsaken for you? Or ill the rock be removed out of its place? \b
“ Yes, the light of the icked ill be put out. The spark of his fire on’t shine.
The light ill be dark in his tent. His lamp above him ill be put out.
The steps of his strength ill be shortened. His on counsel ill cast him don.
For he is cast into a net by his on feet, and he anders into its mesh.
A snare ill take him by the heel. A trap ill catch him.
A noose is hidden for him in the ground, a trap for him on the path.
Terrors ill make him afraid on every side, and ill chase him at his heels.
His strength ill be famished. Calamity ill be ready at his side.
The members of his body ill be devoured. The firstborn of death ill devour his members.
He ill be rooted out of the security of his tent. He ill be brought to the king of terrors.
There ill dell in his tent that hich is none of his. Sulfur ill be scattered on his habitation.
His roots ill be dried up beneath. His branch ill be cut off above.
His memory ill perish from the earth. He ill have no name in the street.
He ill be driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the orld.
He ill have neither son nor grandson among his people, nor any remaining here he lived.
Those ho come after ill be astonished at his day, as those ho ent before ere frightened.
Surely such are the dellings of the unrighteous. This is the place of him ho doesn’t kno God.”
Then Job ansered,
“ Ho long ill you torment me, and crush me ith ords?
You have reproached me ten times. You aren’t ashamed that you attack me.
If it is true that I have erred, my error remains ith myself.
If indeed you ill magnify yourselves against me, and plead against me my reproach,
kno no that God has subverted me, and has surrounded me ith his net. \b
“ Behold, I cry out of rong, but I am not heard. I cry for help, but there is no justice.
He has alled up my ay so that I can’t pass, and has set darkness in my paths.
He has stripped me of my glory, and taken the cron from my head.
He has broken me don on every side, and I am gone. He has plucked my hope up like a tree.
He has also kindled his rath against me. He counts me among his adversaries.
His troops come on together, build a siege ramp against me, and encamp around my tent. \b
“ He has put my brothers far from me. My acquaintances are holly estranged from me.
My relatives have gone aay. My familiar friends have forgotten me.
Those ho dell in my house and my maids consider me a stranger. I am an alien in their sight.
I call to my servant, and he gives me no anser. I beg him ith my mouth.
My breath is offensive to my ife. I am loathsome to the children of my on mother.
Even young children despise me. If I arise, they speak against me.
All my familiar friends abhor me. They hom I loved have turned against me.
My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh. I have escaped by the skin of my teeth. \b
“ Have pity on me. Have pity on me, you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me.
Why do you persecute me as God, and are not satisfied ith my flesh? \b
“ Oh that my ords ere no ritten! Oh that they ere inscribed in a book!
That ith an iron pen and lead they ere engraved in the rock forever!
But as for me, I kno that my Redeemer lives. In the end, he ill stand upon the earth.
After my skin is destroyed, then I ill see God in my flesh,
hom I, even I, ill see on my side. My eyes ill see, and not as a stranger. \b “ My heart is consumed ithin me.
If you say, ’ Ho e ill persecute him!’ because the root of the matter is found in me,
be afraid of the sord, for rath brings the punishments of the sord, that you may kno there is a judgment.”
Then Zophar the Naamathite ansered,
“ Therefore my thoughts anser me, even by reason of my haste that is in me.
I have heard the reproof hich puts me to shame. The spirit of my understanding ansers me.
Don’t you kno this from old time, since man as placed on earth,
that the triumphing of the icked is short, the joy of the godless but for a moment?
Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds,
yet he ill perish forever like his on dung. Those ho have seen him ill say, ’Where is he?’
He ill fly aay as a dream, and ill not be found. Yes, he ill be chased aay like a vision of the night.
The eye hich sa him ill see him no more, neither ill his place see him any more.
His children ill seek the favor of the poor. His hands ill give back his ealth.
His bones are full of his youth, but youth ill lie don ith him in the dust. \b
“Though ickedness is seet in his mouth, though he hide it under his tongue,
though he spare it, and ill not let it go, but keep it still ithin his mouth,
yet his food in his boels is turned. It is cobra venom ithin him.
He has salloed don riches, and he ill vomit them up again. God ill cast them out of his belly.
He ill suck cobra venom. The viper’s tongue ill kill him.
He ill not look at the rivers, the floing streams of honey and butter.
He ill restore that for hich he labored, and ill not sallo it don. He ill not rejoice according to the substance that he has gotten.
For he has oppressed and forsaken the poor. He has violently taken aay a house, and he ill not build it up. \b
“ Because he kne no quietness ithin him, he ill not save anything of that in hich he delights.
There as nothing left that he didn’t devour, therefore his prosperity ill not endure.
In the fullness of his sufficiency, distress ill overtake him. The hand of everyone ho is in misery ill come on him.
When he is about to fill his belly, God ill cast the fierceness of his rath on him. It ill rain on him hile he is eating.
He ill flee from the iron eapon. The bronze arro ill strike him through.
He dras it out, and it comes out of his body. Yes, the glittering point comes out of his liver. Terrors are on him.
All darkness is laid up for his treasures. An unfanned fire ill devour him. It ill consume that hich is left in his tent.
The heavens ill reveal his iniquity. The earth ill rise up against him.
The increase of his house ill depart. They ill rush aay in the day of his rath.
This is the portion of a icked man from God, the heritage appointed to him by God.”
Then Job ansered,
“ Listen diligently to my speech. Let this be your consolation.
Allo me, and I also ill speak. After I have spoken, mock on.
As for me, is my complaint to man? Why shouldn’t I be impatient?
Look at me, and be astonished. Lay your hand on your mouth.
When I remember, I am troubled. Horror takes hold of my flesh. \b
“ Why do the icked live, become old, yes, and gro mighty in poer?
Their child is established ith them in their sight, their offspring before their eyes.
Their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them.
Their bulls breed ithout fail. Their cos calve, and don’t miscarry.
They send out their little ones like a flock. Their children dance.
They sing to the tambourine and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the pipe.
They spend their days in prosperity. In an instant they go don to Sheol.
They tell God, ’ Depart from us, for e don’t ant to kno about your ays.
What is the Almighty, that e should serve him? What profit should e have, if e pray to him?’
Behold, their prosperity is not in their hand. The counsel of the icked is far from me. \b
“ Ho often is it that the lamp of the icked is put out, that their calamity comes on them, that God distributes sorros in his anger?
Ho often is it that they are as stubble before the ind, as chaff that the storm carries aay?
You say, ’ God lays up his iniquity for his children.’ Let him recompense it to himself, that he may kno it.
Let his on eyes see his destruction. Let him drink of the rath of the Almighty.
For hat does he care for his house after him, hen the number of his months is cut off? \b
“ Shall any teach God knoledge, since he judges those ho are high?
One dies in his full strength, being holly at ease and quiet.
His pails are full of milk. The marro of his bones is moistened.
Another dies in bitterness of soul, and never tastes of good.
They lie don alike in the dust. The orm covers them. \b
“ Behold, I kno your thoughts, the plans ith hich you ould rong me.
For you say, ’ Where is the house of the prince? Where is the tent in hich the icked lived?’
Haven’t you asked ayfaring men? Don’t you kno their evidences,
that the evil man is reserved to the day of calamity, that they are led out to the day of rath?
Who ill declare his ay to his face? Who ill repay him hat he has done?
Yet he ill be borne to the grave. Men ill keep atch over the tomb.
The clods of the valley ill be seet to him. All men ill dra after him, as there ere innumerable before him.
So ho can you comfort me ith nonsense, because in your ansers there remains only falsehood?”
Then Eliphaz the Temanite ansered,
“ Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he ho is ise is profitable to himself.
Is it any pleasure to the Almighty that you are righteous? Or does it benefit him that you make your ays perfect?
Is it for your piety that he reproves you, that he enters ith you into judgment?
Isn’t your ickedness great? Neither is there any end to your iniquities.
For you have taken pledges from your brother for nothing, and stripped the naked of their clothing.
You haven’t given ater to the eary to drink, and you have ithheld bread from the hungry.
But as for the mighty man, he had the earth. The honorable man, he lived in it.
You have sent idos aay empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken.
Therefore snares are around you. Sudden fear troubles you,
or darkness, so that you can not see, and floods of aters cover you. \b
“Isn’t God in the heights of heaven? See the height of the stars, ho high they are!
You say, ’ What does God kno? Can he judge through the thick darkness?
Thick clouds are a covering to him, so that he doesn’t see. He alks on the vault of the sky.’
Will you keep the old ay, hich icked men have trodden,
ho ere snatched aay before their time, hose foundation as poured out as a stream,
ho said to God, ’ Depart from us!’ and, ’ What can the Almighty do for us?’
Yet he filled their houses ith good things, but the counsel of the icked is far from me.
The righteous see it, and are glad. The innocent ridicule them,
saying, ’ Surely those ho rose up against us are cut off. The fire has consumed their remnant.’ \b
“ Acquaint yourself ith him no, and be at peace. By it, good ill come to you.
Please receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his ords in your heart.
If you return to the Almighty, you ill be built up, if you put aay unrighteousness far from your tents.
Lay your treasure in the dust, the gold of Ophir among the stones of the brooks.
The Almighty ill be your treasure, and precious silver to you.
For then you ill delight yourself in the Almighty, and ill lift up your face to God.
You ill make your prayer to him, and he ill hear you. You ill pay your vos.
You ill also decree a thing, and it ill be established to you. Light ill shine on your ays.
When they cast don, you ill say, ’ be lifted up.’ He ill save the humble person.
He ill even deliver him ho is not innocent. Yes, he ill be delivered through the cleanness of your hands.”
Then Job ansered,
“ Even today my complaint is rebellious. His hand is heavy in spite of my groaning.
Oh that I kne here I might find him! That I might come even to his seat!
I ould set my cause in order before him, and fill my mouth ith arguments.
I ould kno the ords hich he ould anser me, and understand hat he ould tell me.
Would he contend ith me in the greatness of his poer? No, but he ould listen to me.
There the upright might reason ith him, so I should be delivered forever from my judge. \b
“ If I go east, he is not there. If I go est, I can’t find him.
He orks to the north, but I can’t see him. He turns south, but I can’t catch a glimpse of him. \b
But he knos the ay that I take. When he has tried me, I ill come out like gold.
My foot has held fast to his steps. I have kept his ay, and not turned aay.
I haven’t gone back from the commandment of his lips. I have treasured up the ords of his mouth more than my necessary food.
But he stands alone, and ho can oppose him? What his soul desires, even that he does.
For he performs that hich is appointed for me. Many such things are ith him.
Therefore I am terrified at his presence. When I consider, I am afraid of him.
For God has made my heart faint. The Almighty has terrified me.
Because I as not cut off before the darkness, neither did he cover the thick darkness from my face. \b
“ Why aren’t times laid up by the Almighty? Why don’t those ho kno him see his days?
There are people ho remove the landmarks. They violently take aay flocks, and feed them.
They drive aay the donkey of the fatherless, and they take the ido’s ox for a pledge.
They turn the needy out of the ay. The poor of the earth all hide themselves.
Behold, as ild donkeys in the desert, they go out to their ork, seeking diligently for food. The ilderness yields them bread for their children.
They cut their food in the field. They glean the vineyard of the icked.
They lie all night naked ithout clothing, and have no covering in the cold.
They are et ith the shoers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for lack of a shelter.
There are those ho pluck the fatherless from the breast, and take a pledge of the poor,
so that they go around naked ithout clothing. Being hungry, they carry the sheaves.
They make oil ithin the alls of these men. They tread ine presses, and suffer thirst.
From out of the populous city, men groan. The soul of the ounded cries out, yet God doesn’t regard the folly. \b
“ These are of those ho rebel against the light. They don’t kno its ays, nor stay in its paths.
The murderer rises ith the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief.
The eye also of the adulterer aits for the tilight, saying, ’ No eye ill see me.’ He disguises his face.
In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t kno the light.
For the morning is to all of them like thick darkness, for they kno the terrors of the thick darkness. \b
“ They are foam on the surface of the aters. Their portion is cursed on the earth. They don’t turn into the ay of the vineyards.
Drought and heat consume the sno aters, so does Sheol those ho have sinned.
The omb ill forget him. The orm ill feed seetly on him. He ill be no more remembered. Unrighteousness ill be broken as a tree.
He devours the barren ho don’t bear. He shos no kindness to the ido.
Yet God preserves the mighty by his poer. He rises up ho has no assurance of life.
God gives them security, and they rest in it. His eyes are on their ays.
They are exalted; yet a little hile, and they are gone. Yes, they are brought lo, they are taken out of the ay as all others, and are cut off as the tops of the ears of grain.
If it isn’t so no, ho ill prove me a liar, and make my speech orth nothing?” \b
Then Bildad the Shuhite ansered,
“ Dominion and fear are ith him. He makes peace in his high places.
Can his armies be counted? On hom does his light not arise?
Ho then can man be just ith God? Or ho can he ho is born of a oman be clean?
Behold, even the moon has no brightness, and the stars are not pure in his sight;
Ho much less man, ho is a orm, and the son of man, ho is a orm!”
Then Job ansered,
“ Ho have you helped him ho is ithout poer! Ho have you saved the arm that has no strength!
Ho have you counseled him ho has no isdom, and plentifully declared sound knoledge!
To hom have you uttered ords? Whose spirit came out of you? \b
“ The departed spirits tremble, those beneath the aters and all that live in them.
Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering.
He stretches out the north over empty space, and hangs the earth on nothing.
He binds up the aters in his thick clouds, and the cloud is not burst under them.
He encloses the face of his throne, and spreads his cloud on it.
He has described a boundary on the surface of the aters, and to the confines of light and darkness.
The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his rebuke.
He stirs up the sea ith his poer, and by his understanding he strikes through Rahab.
By his Spirit the heavens are garnished. His hand has pierced the sift serpent.
Behold, these are but the outskirts of his ays. Ho small a hisper do e hear of him! But the thunder of his poer ho can understand?”
Job again took up his parable, and said,
“ As God lives, ho has taken aay my right, the Almighty, ho has made my soul bitter
( for the length of my life is still in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils);
surely my lips ill not speak unrighteousness, neither ill my tongue utter deceit.
Far be it from me that I should justify you. Until I die I ill not put aay my integrity from me.
I hold fast to my righteousness, and ill not let it go. My heart ill not reproach me so long as I live. \b
“ Let my enemy be as the icked. Let him ho rises up against me be as the unrighteous. \b
For hat is the hope of the godless, hen he is cut off, hen God takes aay his life?
Will God hear his cry hen trouble comes on him?
Will he delight himself in the Almighty, and call on God at all times?
I ill teach you about the hand of God. I ill not conceal that hich is ith the Almighty.
Behold, all of you have seen it yourselves; hy then have you become altogether vain? \b
“ This is the portion of a icked man ith God, the heritage of oppressors, hich they receive from the Almighty.
If his children are multiplied, it is for the sord. His offspring ill not be satisfied ith bread.
Those ho remain of him ill be buried in death. His idos ill make no lamentation.
Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare clothing as the clay;
he may prepare it, but the just ill put it on, and the innocent ill divide the silver.
He builds his house as the moth, as a booth hich the atchman makes.
He lies don rich, but he ill not do so again. He opens his eyes, and he is not.
Terrors overtake him like aters. A storm steals him aay in the night.
The east ind carries him aay, and he departs. It seeps him out of his place.
For it hurls at him, and does not spare, as he flees aay from his hand.
Men ill clap their hands at him, and ill hiss him out of his place. \b
“ Surely there is a mine for silver, and a place for gold hich they refine.
Iron is taken out of the earth, and copper is smelted out of the ore.
Man sets an end to darkness, and searches out, to the furthest bound, the stones of obscurity and of thick darkness.
He breaks open a shaft aay from here people live. They are forgotten by the foot. They hang far from men, they sing back and forth.
As for the earth, out of it comes bread. Underneath it is turned up as it ere by fire.
Sapphires come from its rocks. It has dust of gold.
That path no bird of prey knos, neither has the falcon’s eye seen it.
The proud animals have not trodden it, nor has the fierce lion passed by there.
He puts his hand on the flinty rock, and he overturns the mountains by the roots.
He cuts out channels among the rocks. His eye sees every precious thing.
He binds the streams that they don’t trickle. The thing that is hidden he brings out to light. \b
“But here ill isdom be found? Where is the place of understanding?
Man doesn’t kno its price, and it isn’t found in the land of the living.
The deep says, ’ It isn’t in me.’ The sea says, ’ It isn’t ith me.’
It can’t be gotten for gold, neither ill silver be eighed for its price.
It can’t be valued ith the gold of Ophir, ith the precious onyx, or the sapphire.
Gold and glass can’t equal it, neither ill it be exchanged for jeels of fine gold.
No mention ill be made of coral or of crystal. Yes, the price of isdom is above rubies.
The topaz of Ethiopia ill not equal it. It on’t be valued ith pure gold.
Where then does isdom come from? Where is the place of understanding?
Seeing it is hidden from the eyes of all living, and kept close from the birds of the sky.
Destruction and Death say, ’ We have heard a rumor of it ith our ears.’ \b
“God understands its ay, and he knos its place.
For he looks to the ends of the earth, and sees under the hole sky.
He establishes the force of the ind. Yes, he measures out the aters by measure.
When he made a decree for the rain, and a ay for the lightning of the thunder,
then he sa it, and declared it. He established it, yes, and searched it out.
To man he said, ’ Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is isdom. To depart from evil is understanding.’” \b
Job again took up his parable, and said,
“ Oh that I ere as in the months of old, as in the days hen God atched over me;
hen his lamp shone on my head, and by his light I alked through darkness,
as I as in my prime, hen the friendship of God as in my tent,
hen the Almighty as yet ith me, and my children ere around me,
hen my steps ere ashed ith butter, and the rock poured out streams of oil for me,
hen I ent out to the city gate, hen I prepared my seat in the street.
The young men sa me and hid themselves. The aged rose up and stood.
The princes refrained from talking, and laid their hand on their mouth.
The voice of the nobles as hushed, and their tongue stuck to the roof of their mouth.
For hen the ear heard me, then it blessed me, and hen the eye sa me, it commended me,
because I delivered the poor ho cried, and the fatherless also, ho had no one to help him,
the blessing of him ho as ready to perish came on me, and I caused the ido’s heart to sing for joy.
I put on righteousness, and it clothed me. My justice as as a robe and a diadem.
I as eyes to the blind, and feet to the lame.
I as a father to the needy. I researched the cause of him hom I didn’t kno.
I broke the jas of the unrighteous and plucked the prey out of his teeth.
Then I said, ’ I ill die in my on house, I ill count my days as the sand.
My root is spread out to the aters. The de lies all night on my branch.
My glory is fresh in me. My bo is reneed in my hand.’ \b
“Men listened to me, aited, and kept silence for my counsel.
After my ords they didn’t speak again. My speech fell on them.
They aited for me as for the rain. Their mouths drank as ith the spring rain.
I smiled on them hen they had no confidence. They didn’t reject the light of my face.
I chose out their ay, and sat as chief. I lived as a king in the army, as one ho comforts the mourners. \b
“ But no those ho are younger than I have me in derision, hose fathers I considered unorthy to put ith my sheep dogs.
Of hat use is the strength of their hands to me, men in hom ripe age has perished?
They are gaunt from lack and famine. They gna the dry ground, in the gloom of aste and desolation.
They pluck salt herbs by the bushes. The roots of the broom tree are their food.
They are driven out from among men. They cry after them as after a thief,
so that they live in frightful valleys, and in holes of the earth and of the rocks.
They bray among the bushes. They are gathered together under the nettles.
They are children of fools, yes, children of icked men. They ere flogged out of the land. \b
“ No I have become their song. Yes, I am a byord to them.
They abhor me, they stand aloof from me, and don’t hesitate to spit in my face.
For he has untied his cord, and afflicted me; and they have thron off restraint before me.
On my right hand rise the rabble. They thrust aside my feet. They cast their ays of destruction up against me.
They mar my path. They promote my destruction ithout anyone’s help.
As through a ide breach they come. They roll themselves in amid the ruin.
Terrors have turned on me. They chase my honor as the ind. My elfare has passed aay as a cloud. \b
“ No my soul is poured out ithin me. Days of affliction have taken hold of me.
In the night season my bones are pierced in me, and the pains that gna me take no rest.
My garment is disfigured by great force. It binds me about as the collar of my tunic.
He has cast me into the mire. I have become like dust and ashes.
I cry to you, and you do not anser me. I stand up, and you gaze at me.
You have turned to be cruel to me. With the might of your hand you persecute me.
You lift me up to the ind, and drive me ith it. You dissolve me in the storm.
For I kno that you ill bring me to death, to the house appointed for all living. \b
“Hoever doesn’t one stretch out a hand in his fall? Or in his calamity therefore cry for help?
Didn’t I eep for him ho as in trouble? Wasn’t my soul grieved for the needy?
When I looked for good, then evil came. When I aited for light, darkness came.
My heart is troubled, and doesn’t rest. Days of affliction have come on me.
I go mourning ithout the sun. I stand up in the assembly, and cry for help.
I am a brother to jackals, and a companion to ostriches.
My skin gros black and peels from me. My bones are burned ith heat.
Therefore my harp has turned to mourning, and my pipe into the voice of those ho eep. \b
“ I made a covenant ith my eyes; ho then should I look lustfully at a young oman?
For hat is the portion from God above, and the heritage from the Almighty on high?
Is it not calamity to the unrighteous, and disaster to the orkers of iniquity?
Doesn’t he see my ays, and count all my steps? \b
“If I have alked ith falsehood, and my foot has hurried to deceit
(let me be eighed in an even balance, that God may kno my integrity);
if my step has turned out of the ay, if my heart alked after my eyes, if any defilement has stuck to my hands,
then let me so, and let another eat. Yes, let the produce of my field be rooted out. \b
“If my heart has been enticed to a oman, and I have laid ait at my neighbor’s door,
then let my ife grind for another, and let others sleep ith her.
For that ould be a heinous crime. Yes, it ould be an iniquity to be punished by the judges,
for it is a fire that consumes to destruction, and ould root out all my increase.
“If I have despised the cause of my male servant or of my female servant, hen they contended ith me,
hat then ill I do hen God rises up? When he visits, hat ill I anser him?
Didn’t he ho made me in the omb make him? Didn’t one fashion us in the omb?
“If I have ithheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the ido to fail,
or have eaten my morsel alone, and the fatherless has not eaten of it
(no, from my youth he gre up ith me as ith a father, I have guided her from my mother’s omb);
if I have seen any perish for ant of clothing, or that the needy had no covering;
if his heart hasn’t blessed me, if he hasn’t been armed ith my sheep’s fleece;
if I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless, because I sa my help in the gate;
then let my shoulder fall from the shoulder blade, and my arm be broken from the bone.
For calamity from God is a terror to me. Because of his majesty, I can do nothing.
“ If I have made gold my hope, and have said to the fine gold, ’ You are my confidence;’
If I have rejoiced because my ealth as great, and because my hand had gotten much;
if I have seen the sun hen it shined, or the moon moving in splendor,
and my heart has been secretly enticed, and my hand thre a kiss from my mouth;
